families.name: Extractive Summarization
families.definition: Methods that select and concatenate existing sentences or phrases from the source document to form the summary.

properties.text: These methods rely on scoring mechanisms such as TF-IDF, TextRank, or graph-based centrality to rank sentences.
They preserve the original wording of the source text, ensuring factual consistency with the input.
They are computationally efficient and do not require large-scale pre-trained language models.
They are particularly effective for structured medical documents where key information is explicitly stated in discrete sentences.

limitations.text: They often produce disjointed or redundant summaries that lack narrative flow and coherence.
They cannot generate new information or paraphrase content, limiting their ability to handle complex medical reasoning.
They struggle with long documents where the most critical information is distributed across non-adjacent sections.
They are sensitive to noise and irrelevant boilerplate text common in raw medical records.

families.name: Abstractive Summarization
families.definition: Methods that generate new text by understanding the source content and synthesizing it into a coherent, concise summary.

properties.text: These methods utilize sequence-to-sequence architectures, often enhanced with attention mechanisms, to map input tokens to output tokens.
They can paraphrase, compress, and restructure information to create fluent and human-readable summaries.
They are capable of handling unstructured and noisy medical notes by inferring implicit relationships between clinical entities.
They allow for the integration of domain-specific knowledge through fine-tuning on medical corpora.

limitations.text: They are prone to hallucination, generating clinically inaccurate or fabricated details not present in the source.
They require significant computational resources and large, high-quality annotated datasets for effective training.
They often struggle with maintaining strict factual fidelity, which is critical in medical contexts.
They may overlook rare but critical medical terms if the training data is biased toward common conditions.

families.name: Hybrid Approaches
families.definition: Methods that combine extractive and abstractive techniques to leverage the factual grounding of extraction with the fluency of generation.

properties.text: These methods typically use an extractive module to identify key sentences and an abstractive module to refine and connect them.
They aim to mitigate hallucination by constraining the generative model to the extracted evidence.
They can incorporate knowledge graphs or ontologies to ensure semantic consistency in the generated summary.
They are designed to balance the trade-off between factual accuracy and linguistic quality.

limitations.text: They are more complex to design, train, and deploy than single-paradigm approaches.
The performance is often limited by the weaker of the two components (extraction or generation).
They may still suffer from partial hallucinations if the abstractive component deviates from the extracted constraints.
They require careful tuning of the interaction between the extractive and abstractive stages.

families.name: Knowledge-Enhanced Summarization
families.definition: Methods that integrate external medical knowledge bases, ontologies, or knowledge graphs to guide the summarization process.

properties.text: These methods use medical ontologies like UMLS or SNOMED CT to normalize and interpret clinical terms.
They can identify and prioritize clinically significant entities and relationships that may be missed by statistical methods.
They improve the domain-specific accuracy and relevance of the summary by grounding it in established medical knowledge.
They can handle ambiguous or rare medical terminology by leveraging external semantic resources.

limitations.text: They depend on the quality, coverage, and up-to-dateness of the external knowledge bases.
Integrating knowledge graphs adds significant complexity to the model architecture and inference pipeline.
They may introduce biases if the external knowledge base is incomplete or outdated.
They are less adaptable to novel medical conditions or emerging terminologies not yet captured in the knowledge base.
Ensuring strict factual consistency and minimizing hallucinations in abstractive summaries remains a critical challenge.
Developing robust evaluation metrics that capture clinical utility and safety, beyond standard BLEU or ROUGE scores, is an ongoing need.
Handling the privacy and security constraints of sensitive patient data during model training and inference is a major barrier to deployment.
Adapting summarization models to diverse and rapidly evolving medical domains, such as genomics or mental health, requires further research.
Improving the interpretability of summarization models to allow clinicians to trust and verify the generated summaries is an open problem.
Efficiently processing long-form medical documents, such as full electronic health records, without losing critical context is a technical challenge.
